AuXSpec: Learning to Autoformalize Program
Specifications via Executable Postconditions

Haocheng Wang    Weixuan Yuan    Florian Hübler    Yinya Huang    Zhijiang Guo   Sorrachai Yingchareonthawornchai   Rasmus Kyng Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, ETH Zurich  HKUST(GZ)  HKUST Affiliation: ETH AI Center  Institute for Theoretical Studies, ETH Zurich
Abstract

Formal specifications define intended program behavior and underpin verification, but writing them in theorem provers such as Lean is slow and expertise-intensive, making specification a major bottleneck to scaling formally correct code. Autoformalization from natural-language problems is promising, yet training specification models requires scalable feedback on whether generated specifications capture intended behavior. Prior approaches obtain this feedback through explicit proofs or separately implemented code with formal correspondence proofs, both expensive. We introduce AuXSpec, a Lean framework that pairs declarative postconditions with executable counterparts, obtained through type class resolution when possible and otherwise defined separately with an equivalence proof. Test cases can then evaluate declarative specifications by execution, letting us use agreement as a reinforcement-learning reward. Using AuXSpec, we synthesize 3,037 LeetCode problems and expand training to 19.5K samples through expert iteration on Codeforces. Experiments show that training Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B with the execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 on AuXSpec-Test 0.7% →\rightarrow 82.7% and 14.3% →\rightarrow 84.3%, and the 27B model outperforms all frontier models. On the out-of-domain Verina benchmark with its original prompts, both models improve 7.0% →\rightarrow 90.5% and 21.9% →\rightarrow 90.5% and surpass VeriSpecGen-30B-A3B, the prior state of the art among open-source specification models, on pass@1 (theirs 47.6% vs. ours 73.7% and 84.5%) and pass@4 (theirs 63.9% at pass@10 vs. ours 90.5%). We release the weights of the trained 9B and 27B models and the 3,037 problems with test cases, including the 300-problem AuXSpec-Test benchmark with expert review and correctness proofs for future evaluation.

Models and data: huggingface.co/collections/eth-algopt/auxspec
Website: auxspec.org

1 Introduction

Formal program specifications define the correct behavior of a program over all valid inputs, providing the reference against which implementations can be proved correct or tested. Yet writing such specifications in an interactive theorem prover requires substantial expertise and effort, making specification a fundamental barrier to scaling formal code verification and generation. As AI models make rapid progress in generating code and proving its correctness, this barrier becomes increasingly important: realizing the promise of formally correct code requires automating specification itself. Autoformalization from natural-language programming problems offers a path forward, but immediately raises a central question: when does a generated formal specification faithfully capture the intended problem?

This question is particularly important in modern code-generation pipelines. Large language models (LLMs) can generate solutions to programming problems (e.g., LeetCode) from natural-language descriptions. These solutions can be evaluated using input-output test cases, which provide scalable reward signals for reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2025; Ruan et al., 2026). However, passing test cases does not guarantee correctness, as a solution may still fail on untested inputs (Shi et al., 2026). Formal verification offers a stronger guarantee. Given a specification, which consists of a precondition defining valid inputs and a postcondition characterizing correct outputs (Endres et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026), a theorem prover like Lean can formally prove that an implementation satisfies its specification for every valid input. This guarantee depends on the specification correctly capturing the natural-language problem, yet producing such specifications at scale remains difficult. Manually curating specifications requires substantial expert effort: Clever and Verina contain only 161 and 189 problems, respectively (Thakur et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026a). Automated methods can scale further, but may produce incorrect specifications (Dougherty & Mehta, 2025; Bursuc et al., 2026; Dougherty et al., 2026). Scaling specification therefore requires more than generating formal statements. It also requires efficient and scalable feedback on whether generated specifications match the source problem, analogous to the test-case feedback used to train code-generation models.

Training specification generators has been explored in auto-active verification languages, where a verifier, like an SMT solver, provides the reward by checking candidate specifications on test cases (Yan et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Baksys et al., 2025). However, SMT solvers limit the complexity of specifications that can be checked (Yang et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026a), motivating the use of interactive theorem provers such as Lean. In Lean, prior work checks generated specifications by turning each test case into a theorem to be proved, a method known as symbolic specification testing (Lahiri, 2024; Ye et al., 2026b; Yang et al., 2026). These theorems can require nontrivial proofs, especially when the specification involves unbounded quantifiers. If a proof cannot be found, the test case may be left unresolved or evaluated by an LLM judge. Thus, unlike in code generation (Wang et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), test cases do not directly provide cheap rewards for training specification generators in Lean (Table 1).

To address this issue, we propose AuXSpec, a framework for training models to generate program specifications in Lean 4. AuXSpec retains a declarative postcondition that specifies correctness independently of the implementation and pairs it with an executable postcondition for evaluating test cases, a pairing with a long history in formal methods (Section 6). For each synthesized problem, we prove a postcondition equivalence theorem, separately from generation (Section 2), showing that the two postconditions agree for every valid input. This theorem allows us to evaluate any number of test cases by direct execution in Lean, without proving each case separately.

We build a synthesis pipeline to generate Lean specifications and implementations for 3,037 LeetCode problems. For model training, we combine synthesized data from LeetCode and Codeforces with expert iteration to obtain 19.5K samples for supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

We fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B on these samples and then apply reinforcement learning (RL) with our execution-based reward on 13,637 tasks over 8,579 further problems. The resulting AuXSpec-9B and AuXSpec-27B models can generate and repair both specifications and implementations. Relative to its base model, AuXSpec-27B improves SpecGen pass@4 from 14.3% to 84.3% on AuXSpec-Test and from 21.9% to 90.5% on Verina with its original prompts. The corresponding improvements for AuXSpec-9B are from 0.7% to 82.7% and from 7.0% to 90.5%. Moreover, RL with our execution-based reward improves SpecGen pass@4 over SFT alone for both model sizes (Section 5.4).

Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    Executable specification format. We introduce a specification format that pairs a declarative postcondition with an executable Boolean postcondition, obtained through type class resolution in Lean when a decidability instance exists and defined separately otherwise. A postcondition equivalence theorem proves that the two agree on valid inputs (Section 2).

  • •

    AuXSpec dataset and AuXSpec-Test. We release the 3,037 LeetCode problems with specifications, implementations, frozen test cases and postcondition equivalence proofs, including AuXSpec-Test, an expert-reviewed subset of 300 problems that serves as a benchmark for Lean specification generation (Sections 3 and 3.3).

  • •

    AuXSpec-9B-RL and AuXSpec-27B-RL. Using our execution-based reward, we train and release open-weight models that generate and repair Lean specifications and implementations from natural-language descriptions. AuXSpec-27B-RL surpasses all frontier models in domain, and both models surpass the prior state of the art among open-source specification models on Verina (Tables 4 and 5).

2 Problem formulation

In our autoformalization setup, we represent each programming problem with a Lean file. This section describes the file format, the generation and repair tasks over its components, and the acceptance criteria used in data synthesis, model training and evaluation.

Format. For each programming problem, we take a natural-language problem description, input constraints, and test cases as input, and aim to produce a Lean file containing a specification, an implementation, two theorem statements, and executable tests (Figures 13 and 15a in Appendix G.2.1). The specification consists of a precondition defining valid inputs, a declarative postcondition characterizing correct outputs independently of how they are computed, and an executable postcondition that expresses the same condition in a form that can be directly evaluated on test cases by Lean. The implementation is an algorithm that computes an output from a given input. The file also contains two theorems: the postcondition equivalence theorem, asserting that the two postconditions agree on valid inputs, and the correctness theorem, asserting that the implementation satisfies the declarative postcondition. We include the test cases in the Lean file as #guard commands that check the precondition, the executable postcondition and the implementation. We illustrate the format with two synthesized problems, Count Number of Special Subsequences and Continuous Subarray Sum (Appendix G.2.1).

Tasks. We train our models on specification generation (SpecGen) and code generation (CodeGen), as in prior work (Ye et al., 2026a), and their repair variants, SpecGen-Repair and CodeGen-Repair (Table 2). The synthesis pipeline performs these tasks and assembles the generated components into complete Lean files to build the training data and test set.

Acceptance criteria. We apply a common set of acceptance criteria for data filtering, expert iteration, reinforcement learning and evaluation. A generated output is accepted only if the assembled file compiles, the task-specific test layers pass, and LLM judges approve (Zheng et al., 2023).

Test cases are fixed before synthesis and executed as #guard commands, which fail at compilation when the expression is false. The commands are organized into layers by component and type of test (Table 7 in Appendix A.2), and the generated commands must match the frozen test cases. Beyond the test cases, LLM judges check faithfulness (whether the postcondition captures the problem’s requirements), non-tautology (whether the postcondition characterizes correct outputs rather than restating a solution algorithm), completeness (whether the executable postcondition accepts correct outputs on untested inputs) and termination (whether the implementation terminates on valid inputs).

Proofs. The Lean file includes two theorem statements, whose proofs are left as sorry throughout data synthesis, training, and evaluation. We instead adopt executable tests and LLM judges as acceptance criteria, and assess the reliability of these checks separately. For 35.5% of the synthesized problems, the executable postcondition is obtained directly through decidability instances and agrees with the declarative postcondition by construction. After synthesis, we attempt to prove postcondition equivalence for all 3,037 problems, and 99.0% are provable without modifying their definitions (Section 3.2), which indicates that the proofs expose errors beyond tests and judges in only 1.0% of the synthesized problems. The remaining problems are repaired and then proved. For model-generated specifications, we also validate acceptance by proof, and the postcondition equivalence theorem holds for 99.2% of accepted outputs of both RL models (Appendix H.4). We note that the proved theorem shows only that the two postconditions agree, but both may encode the same misunderstanding: expert review finds 9 such errors among the 300 AuXSpec-Test problems (Appendix I.1). Semantic agreement with the problem therefore rests on the test cases, the judges and expert review (Section 3.3).

We do not require correctness proofs for generated implementations either, since such proofs are long (a median of about 160 lines on AuXSpec-Test, Appendix H.3) and implementation verification is not the focus of this work. We nevertheless prove correctness for all 300 AuXSpec-Test problems to provide verified references for evaluation (Section 3.3).

3 Data synthesis

To train and evaluate models on the tasks defined in Section 2, we synthesize and release 3,037 LeetCode problems in our Lean format. The dataset provides training data and includes a held-out, expert-reviewed set of 300 problems, AuXSpec-Test, for evaluation. In this section, we describe the synthesis pipeline, report its results and introduce AuXSpec-Test.

3.1 Synthesis pipeline

Our pipeline takes a problem description and test cases as input (Figure 1). We first make a problem-level plan, then generate the declarative specification (the precondition and the declarative postcondition), the executable postcondition, and the implementation in three stages. In each stage, we plan and generate a component, validate it against the acceptance criteria of Section 2 and repair it if validation fails. We separate the stages to prevent the generation of a later component from overfitting the test cases or weakening an accepted specification (Baksys et al., 2025). Finally, we assemble the accepted components into a Lean file in the format of Section 2.

Inputs. We collect 3,109 LeetCode problems (Xia et al., 2025) with typed function signatures, reference solutions, and existing test cases (Table 3). Before synthesis, we construct and freeze positive and negative test cases for each problem (Appendix G.1.1). A positive test case pairs a valid input with the output of the reference solution, which is computed independently of the specifications under synthesis (Wang et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; He et al., 2026). A negative test case is either an invalid input or a valid input paired with an incorrect output.

Specification. We first generate the precondition and the declarative postcondition. To make the declarative postcondition executable, we apply decide when a decidability instance is available and otherwise attempt to synthesize such an instance (Appendix G.2). The result, called the decidable form, agrees with the declarative postcondition by construction. When instance synthesis fails, the declarative postcondition is reformulated into a separate executable postcondition, and the postcondition equivalence theorem, proved after synthesis (Section 3.2), states that the executable postcondition agrees with the declarative postcondition.

Implementation. Given the accepted specification, we plan an algorithm and generate the implementation, where LLM judges check that the implementation terminates on all valid inputs and is fast enough for the stated constraints (Appendix G.3.1).

Repair. If a component fails validation, the model revises it from compiler errors, failed test cases and judge feedback for up to 18 rounds. Each repair round modifies only the faulty code block, leaving other blocks and accepted components unchanged, which prevents repairs from weakening a specification to pass the test cases. The recorded repairs provide the repair samples of Section 4.1.

Models. Based on a pilot comparison of frontier models (Appendix G.8), we select Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team, 2026) for generation and repair, DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) for planning, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash for the judges.

3.2 Results

The pipeline synthesizes 3,037 of the 3,109 problems (97.7%, Appendix G.5). Only 34.8% of the problems pass all stages at the first attempt, and repair recovers most of the others within 2 rounds (Appendix G.4.1). For 35.5% of the synthesized problems, the declarative postcondition can be made executable by decide. These executable postconditions pass validation on the first attempt in 98.1% of cases, compared with 52.4% for those generated separately (Appendix G.2.2). Since tests on small inputs do not detect nontermination or inefficiency, the implementation judge rejects 19.6% of the generated implementations that pass all test cases (Appendix G.3.1).

After synthesis, we attempt to prove the postcondition equivalence theorem for all 3,037 problems (Appendix H), and the attempts expose statement errors in 31 problems (1.0%), all of which had passed the test layers and the judges. Most of these errors (19) are in the declarative postcondition, which execution never evaluates (Table 39 in Appendix H). We repair the 31 problems and then prove the theorem. For the remaining 99.0% of the problems, the theorem is provable as synthesized.

3.3 AuXSpec-Test

AuXSpec-Test is a held-out evaluation benchmark consisting of 300 problems from the synthesized dataset, with 72 easy, 155 medium and 73 hard problems, yielding 834 samples across four tasks (Table 11 in Appendix C.3). We manually review every component against the problem description and identify errors in 21 problems (Appendix I.1). Attempts to prove the correctness theorems reveal one additional error (Appendix H.3). We correct these 22 problems and prove correctness for all 300; the remaining 278 problems (92.7%) require no changes to their definitions.

These reviewed problems serve as references for evaluating model-generated specifications and implementations. For SpecGen, we pair a generated specification with the reference implementation, and for CodeGen, a generated implementation with the reference specification. The repair tasks are evaluated in the same way, and we check the resulting Lean files against the acceptance criteria of Section 2. Since evaluation relies on test cases and judges rather than comparison with the reference specification, it can accept alternative correct formulations.

4 Training

4.1 Training data

Each synthesized problem contributes samples to the tasks of Section 2. The generation tasks take accepted components as targets, and the repair tasks take components rejected during synthesis as inputs. To obtain a starting point for RL that reasons concisely, we rephrase the long and often redundant reasoning recorded during synthesis into a short trace of the planning behind a generated component or the diagnosis behind a repair (Appendix G.6).

Increasing the number of problems improves SpecGen performance more than continued pretraining on a Mathlib corpus (Appendix E.2). We therefore source further problems for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) from Codeforces, AtCoder, Aizu, CodeChef and GeeksforGeeks through TACO (Li et al., 2023) and open-r1/codeforces (Penedo et al., 2025) (Table 3). To eliminate the risk of data contamination, the final SFT and RL data are disjoint from each other and from the evaluation benchmarks (Appendix C).

4.2 Supervised fine-tuning

We expand the SFT data to 19.5K training samples over 3 rounds of expert iteration (Polu et al., 2023), each fine-tuning Qwen3.8-27B from the base model on the accumulated samples and adding the outputs that meet the acceptance criteria of Section 2. SpecGen performance rises as the data grow, with no sign of saturation (Appendix E.1). Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a) and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b) on these samples yields AuXSpec-9B-SFT and AuXSpec-27B-SFT, with the settings of Appendix B.

4.3 Reinforcement learning

We further apply RL to the SFT models for 1 epoch on 13,637 SpecGen and CodeGen tasks over 8,579 problems disjoint from the SFT data and AuXSpec-Test (Table 3), yielding AuXSpec-9B-RL and AuXSpec-27B-RL. We ablate the components of our recipe (Appendix F.2) and compare with VeriSpecGen on the same backbone (Appendix F.1).

Reward design. Since the SFT models solve only 10.1% and 18.7% of SpecGen problems at pass@1 (Section 5.2), a binary reward that requires all acceptance criteria induces low reward variance, which slows optimization even when the reward is faithful to the acceptance criteria (Razin et al., 2025). We therefore score each rollout with a 6-stage progressive reward that follows the order of the acceptance criteria of Section 2 (Le et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2026). Failing a stage assigns the rollout the value of that stage, from format (0), compilation (0.1), test execution (0.2), test case alignment (0.1), non-tautology (0.1) to overall quality (0.4), and passing all stages yields 1. With vkv_{k} the value of stage kk, the reward of rollout yy is

r⁡(y)={1if ​y​ passes all stages,vkif ​k​ is the first stage that ​y​ fails.r(y)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }y\text{ passes all stages,}\\ v_{k}&\text{if }k\text{ is the first stage that }y\text{ fails.}\end{cases} (1)

We value non-tautology at 0.1 to rank specifications that restate the computation without specifying the problem below failed tests. Replaying the training rollouts shows that at this value tautological specifications have a negative mean advantage in every group, whereas at a higher value such as 0.3 the advantage turns positive in groups where no rollout passes (Appendix E.3.2). Two kinds of rollouts that pass all stages receive partial credit instead of 1, enumerative specifications (0.4) and slow implementations (0.5), which evaluation accepts. To prevent reward hacking, a test counts toward the required number of tests only if it calls a declaration of the output, which excludes tests that hold trivially. Falling short of this number reduces the reward to 0.1. Hard-coding answers, by special-casing the test inputs or by copying the given test cases into the implementation, sets the reward to 0, and so does returning a repair unchanged (Appendix E.3.1).

Self-repair. Besides generation, we train on repair tasks built from failed rollouts of the current policy, which avoids distribution shift (Kumar et al., 2025). During training, these failed rollouts are paired with compiler messages or judge feedback in a buffer, from which 40% of each batch is drawn as single-turn repair tasks (Table 2). Repairs continue for up to 3 rounds, and the reward of a repair rollout is scaled down linearly from 1 in the first round to 0.8 in the last.

Policy optimization. Our RL algorithm extends Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (Yu et al., 2025, DAPO;) by normalizing the advantage by the standard deviation over the batch instead of the group (Hu et al., 2025) and masking the clipped surrogate ℓi,t\ell_{i,t} of token tt in rollout ii with mi,t∈{0,1}m_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}. We maximize

𝒥⁡(θ)=𝔼⁡[∑i,tmi,t​ℓi,t​(θ)∑i,tmi,t],\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{\sum_{i,t}m_{i,t}\,\ell_{i,t}(\theta)}{\sum_{i,t}m_{i,t}}\Big], (2)

which reduces to the original algorithm with mi,t=1m_{i,t}=1 and group normalization. We classify a rollout as repetitive if a 40-character n-gram occurs at least 20 times and over 40% of n-grams are repeats (Welleck et al., 2020). Repetitive rollouts that reach the length limit receive reward 0, and the mask removes the gradient of such a rollout beyond 200 tokens past the repetition onset. For the 27B model, the loss adds a penalty with weight 0.1 on the probability of the end-of-sequence token inside the thinking segment where it exceeds 1e-6. Appendix B lists the other hyperparameters.

5 Experiments

5.1 Setup

Training settings, including hyperparameters and the Lean environment, are listed in Appendix B, and the sampling settings in Appendix B.2. We report pass@kk for k∈{1,4}k\in\{1,4\}, the fraction of problems with at least one of kk samples meeting the acceptance criteria of Section 2 (Appendix D.1). All evaluated models receive the same prompts (Appendix K). The baselines are our backbones, frontier models and prior work on specification generation.

  • •

    Instruct Models: To isolate the effect of fine-tuning, we evaluate the backbones Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a) and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b).

  • •

    Frontier Models: Claude-Opus-5 (Anthropic, 2026a), Claude-Sonnet-5 (Anthropic, 2026b), GPT-5.6-Sol and GPT-5.6-Luna (OpenAI, 2026), Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), and DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026).

  • •

    Prior Work: We compare against VeriSpecGen (Ye et al., 2026b), which fine-tunes Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B on refinement trajectories distilled from a closed teacher, using the reported results as the models are not publicly available.

5.2 Main results

We report the performance on the in-domain test set in Table 4. Training improves SpecGen pass@4 from 0.7% to 82.7% for the 9B backbone and from 14.3% to 84.3% for the 27B backbone. AuXSpec-27B-RL surpasses every frontier model in both pass@1 and pass@4 on SpecGen and CodeGen, with 65.7% SpecGen pass@1 (vs. 57.7% for Claude-Opus-5, the strongest frontier model). The 9B RL model also outperforms every frontier model in SpecGen pass@1 (58.6%). On the repair tasks, the 27B RL model attains the best CodeGen-Repair pass@1 (88.1%) and stays within 2 points of the best result on the other metrics, while the 9B RL model surpasses most frontier models in SpecGen-Repair pass@1. To assess false positives of SpecGen acceptance, we prove the postcondition equivalence theorem for 99.2% of accepted RL outputs (Appendix H.4), and expert review confirms 90 of 100 sampled outputs, with all errors in the validity predicate (Appendix I.2).

5.3 Out-of-domain evaluation

To assess generalization beyond the synthesized data, we evaluate on Verina (Ye et al., 2026a), a 189-problem manually curated benchmark with reference specifications, implementations and test cases. Following the original evaluation, generated specifications must be sound and complete with respect to the reference specification on the test cases, and generated implementations must pass all positive test cases. AuXSpec-27B-RL outperforms all baselines in SpecGen pass@1 with 91.9% and trails the best baseline in pass@4 by 1.1 points (Table 5). On CodeGen, both RL models outperform all baselines, with pass@1 of 92.6% for the 9B model and 91.8% for the 27B model (vs. 56.6% for the best baseline). The 9B model also attains the highest pass@4 (98.4%). Including the test cases in the prompt improves SpecGen pass@4 of both RL models from 90.5% to 96.8%, and the same test cases improve the pass@4 of frontier models by 5 to 24 points (Table 5).

We further evaluate general capabilities on AIME 25 (Mathematical Association of America, 2025), GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024), and HumanEval+ and MBPP+ (Liu et al., 2023) with the sampling settings of DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025). Supervised fine-tuning lowers every score, and RL recovers about half or more of each drop, with AuXSpec-9B-RL surpassing its backbone on both code benchmarks (Appendix D.3).

Besides providing additional learning signal during training, the repair tasks enable the model to iteratively refine its specifications based on previous outputs and feedback from the compiler and judges at test time. On ICPC-Eval (Xu et al., 2025b), a benchmark of problems from 11 recent contests of the International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC), AuXSpec-27B-RL solves a higher percentage of problems with refine@16 (82.7%) than with pass@16 (61.3%, Appendix D.4).

5.4 RL analysis

Reinforcement learning from the SFT models improves SpecGen pass@1 on AuXSpec-Test from 10.1% to 58.6% for the 9B model and from 18.7% to 65.7% for the 27B model (Table 4 and Figure 2a), and the gains transfer to Verina, where SpecGen pass@1 rises from 37.3% to 87.0% and from 57.3% to 91.9% (Table 5 and Figure 2b). The reward is computed on the synthesized problems only, yet Verina scores each specification against the reference specification on test cases absent from the prompt, so the policy learns faithfulness to the description beyond the frozen test cases.

Gains at pass@1 can also come from sharpening the sampling distribution, in which case the SFT model would catch up at large kk (Yue et al., 2025). SpecGen pass@256 of AuXSpec-27B-SFT (85.7%) stays below pass@8 of AuXSpec-27B-RL (88.2%), and the SFT model therefore needs more than 32 times the samples of the RL model to reach this pass rate. Within 256 samples, 33 of the 300 problems are solved only by the RL model and 1 only by the SFT model (Appendix E.3.3). The RL model is also token-efficient, requiring 20.3% of the output tokens per solved SpecGen sample of the most economical frontier model (Appendix D.2).

We utilize a progressive reward to assign fine-grained credit to partial progress. A binary reward assigns 0 to every rollout that fails any stage and provides no signal in groups where no sample passes. With fine-grained values, the group-relative advantage can distinguish better samples from worse ones within a group, which raises the probability of the better samples until the group saturates. Replaying the rollouts of the final runs confirms the denser signal. Groups without a passing rollout make up 37% of SpecGen groups for the 27B model and 47% for the 9B model and would be discarded by dynamic sampling under a binary reward (Yu et al., 2025), whereas the progressive reward yields nonzero variance in 87.9% and 86.2% of them (Appendix E.3.1). The rollouts shift accordingly and follow this group-relative credit. In the early stage, few CodeGen groups contain a fast and correct program, where slow but correct programs receive a positive advantage and grow (up to 67.4% of correct CodeGen rollouts of the 27B model). These slow programs then decrease gradually as fast programs appear (0.4% at the end), whereas the 9B model, which solves fewer CodeGen problems, ends with more of them (30.4%). Enumerative specifications show a similar pattern (17.0% to 2.8% of otherwise accepted specifications for the 27B model, Figure 2c).

The selection of the intermediate values relies on the reward dynamics, which we measure by replaying the training rollouts and recording the advantage of each stage in groups of different strength. For instance, correct but slow implementations are valued at 0.5, at which their advantage is positive only in groups with fewer than two passing rollouts, whereas at 0.8 it would stay positive with six passing rollouts of 16 (Appendix E.3.2). As CodeGen groups without a passing rollout fall from 44% to 0% over training (Figure 4b2), the mean advantage of slow implementations turns from +0.10+0.10 to −0.17-0.17 (steps 1–40 and 161–208). In SpecGen, 29% to 52% of groups remain without a passing rollout in each period (Figure 4b1), so hard SpecGen problems contribute a learning signal throughout training.

6 Related work

Specification generation. Specification autoformalization translates requirements into formal specifications. Prior work studies postcondition generation from natural language (Endres et al., 2024), executable Python specifications (Chen et al., 2026) and user intent in Dafny (Lahiri, 2024).

Training for specification generation. Training for program specification generation has concentrated on auto-active verification languages (Section 1). In Lean and Rocq, prior work checks a specification by proving each test case separately or by searching for counterexamples (Feng et al., 2026), and reinforcement learning from verifier feedback has targeted correctness proofs (Li et al., 2026b) but remains underexplored for specification generation (Baksys et al., 2025). Specification generators there are trained instead on synthesized and repaired examples, where a reference implementation labels tests, a proof attempt checks each labeled test, and LLM judgments guide refinement when proof automation is inconclusive (Ye et al., 2026b). AuXSpec also labels tests with reference solutions, and relies on the test results of the executable postcondition to filter the training data and to define the reinforcement-learning reward (Section 2).

Executable specifications. The executability of specifications has long been debated in formal methods. Executable specifications can be validated against intended behavior by execution (Kemmerer, 1985; Fuchs, 1992), whereas declarative specifications are more expressive and independent of any algorithm (Hayes & Jones, 1989). Runtime assertion checking and property-based testing run contracts and properties as tests (Meyer, 1992; Cheon & Leavens, 2002; Claessen & Hughes, 2000), and proof assistants test conjectures before proving them (Berghofer & Nipkow, 2004; Lean Community, 2024). Boolean reflection pairs a proposition with a Boolean function and a proof that the two agree (Gonthier & Mahboubi, 2010; Paraskevopoulou et al., 2015). Executable counterparts can also be derived automatically from inductive relations in proof assistants, but the derivation covers a restricted class of relations, and users still write executable variants by hand and prove that the two agree (Berghofer et al., 2009; Paraskevopoulou et al., 2022). AuXSpec utilizes both sides of this trade-off, where we let models generate the executable variants, a step that previously required manual curation.

Adjacent settings. Generating specifications for existing implementations utilizes a verifier to check the specification against the code but assumes the code is correct (Chen et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026). In this setting, reinforcement learning has included executable checks on mutated-output tests in the reward (Huang et al., 2026). Our SpecGen task instead starts from the problem description, input constraints and tests, without access to an implementation. Vericoding benchmarks evaluate the reverse task, generating implementations and proofs from a given formal specification (Zhao et al., 2026; Bursuc et al., 2026).

7 Conclusion

We presented AuXSpec, a framework for training models to generate program specifications in Lean with execution-based feedback. AuXSpec pairs each declarative postcondition with an executable postcondition, and the postcondition equivalence theorem states that both agree on all valid inputs. This allows us to evaluate specifications by directly executing test cases, without proving each case separately. At the same time, we retain the declarative postcondition for formal correctness proofs. With this format, we synthesize and release 3,037 LeetCode problems, each with a proved postcondition equivalence theorem. The dataset includes AuXSpec-Test, a held-out benchmark of 300 expert-reviewed problems, all with proved correctness theorems.

Training on the synthesized data with an execution-based reinforcement-learning reward yields 9B and 27B models, and the 27B model surpasses all frontier models on AuXSpec-Test and outperforms all baselines in SpecGen pass@1 on the out-of-domain Verina benchmark. Since the models are trained only on synthesized problems, the gains on Verina suggest that training with the reward improves faithfulness to the problem description beyond the test cases used in the reward. We discuss the limitations of this work in Appendix J.

AI use statement

We used generative AI tools to synthesize the dataset and to produce proofs. The pipeline uses LLMs to synthesize, repair, judge and rewrite specifications and implementations (Section 3, Appendices G and K), and proof agents built on LLMs produce the postcondition equivalence and correctness proofs, which the Lean kernel checks (Appendix H). We did not use generative AI tools to develop the conceptual framework or to interpret results, and translation and qualitative data analysis do not apply to this work. We also used generative AI tools to edit the text, create figures, search the literature and format references. We reviewed all AI-assisted work, ran the AI-generated code, checked every number against the script that computed it and every citation against the original publication, and take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Ethics statement

One of the authors carried out the expert review of AuXSpec-Test, and 2 of the authors reviewed the accepted outputs (Appendix I), and the work involves no other human participants and no personal data. The problems come from LeetCodeDataset (Xia et al., 2025) and TACO (Li et al., 2023), both released under the Apache-2.0 license, with the web-crawled problem statements of TACO under CC BY 4.0. We use them for research with attribution and will release our data and models under compatible licenses. The released models generate specifications and implementations for programming problems, and every accepted implementation remains checkable by proof against the postcondition.

Reproducibility statement

The synthesis pipeline is described in Section 3, with every stage in Appendix G, the counts at each step in Appendix G.5, the models used in Appendix G.8, condensed prompts of the stages and judges in Appendix K, and the proving of the postcondition equivalence and correctness theorems in Appendix H. Training is described in Section 4, with the training and sampling settings in Appendices B and B.2, expert iteration in Appendix E.1, the metrics in Appendix D.1 and the reinforcement-learning reward and ablations in Appendix E.3. We will release the synthesized problems with test cases and postcondition equivalence proofs, AuXSpec-Test with correctness proofs, the evaluation code and the model weights.
