Appendix A File format

A.1 Declarations

Each term of the paper is implemented by a declaration (Table 6).

A.2 Format

Each file includes precondition, postcondition and executable postcondition with postcondition equivalence theorem, implementation with correctness theorem, and test cases. Helper definitions follow a topological order of dependency. The namespace, the type abbreviations, the printed expressions of the frozen test cases, and both theorem statements are assembled. The test cases are organized into test layers (Table 7).

Appendix B Configuration

B.1 Training

Both model sizes are fine-tuned with the settings in Table 9. AuXSpec-9B-SFT is fine-tuned on an earlier version of the SFT data with 18,489 samples over 4,026 problems. In a round of expert iteration, the model is fine-tuned for 3 epochs on the training samples of that round. Checkpoints are evaluated after each epoch, and the models reported in the main text are the third-epoch checkpoints. Loss is taken on assistant tokens only.

Reinforcement learning follows the settings of Table 9 for 1 epoch of the 13,637 tasks, which takes 434 steps for the 9B model and 208 steps for the 27B model. Rollout and training share the same GPUs, the Lean compilation pool runs on the CPUs of the same nodes, and the LLM judges are called through an external API. Rollouts longer than 12,288 tokens lose reward linearly, up to 1.0 at the limit of 16,384 tokens, following the soft overlong punishment of DAPO (Yu et al., 2025). The optimizer is AdamW with weight decay 0.01 and gradient clipping at 1.0, and the clipped surrogate adds dual clipping with constant 3.0 for negative advantages. The maximum prompt length is 8,192 tokens. A SpecGen rollout needs 12 tests and a CodeGen rollout 3, fewer for problems with fewer test rows. A rollout fails compilation when a declaration does not elaborate, a test cannot be evaluated, compilation exceeds the time limit, the compiler reports an error without a position, or the rollout contains sorry outside the two theorem statements, admit, axiom or native_decide. A rollout receives 0.3 when a judge call fails (Table 19). A rollout is repetitive when a 40-character n-gram, taken at a stride of 4 characters, occurs at least 20 times and fewer than 60% of the n-grams are distinct.

B.2 Inference

Expert iteration, the evaluation of our models and the analyses of Appendix E sample with the settings of Table 10. Baselines follow the sampling settings recommended for each model with the same maximum output length, except the long-reasoning models DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Kimi-K3, which run without a length limit.

Appendix C Training data

C.1 Source selection

The LeetCode problems combine 2,869 problems of LeetCodeDataset (Xia et al., 2025) with 746 free problems collected from the site after the dataset snapshot. Of the 746 problems, 263 pass a buildability filter that requires at least 3 examples and a Python function signature and excludes database, shell, concurrency and design problems. The seeds are 3,109 problems, 2,864 from LeetCodeDataset and 245 from the site. We take the Codeforces and AtCoder problems from the train split of TACO (Li et al., 2023). For RL, we add problems from the train and test splits of TACO, including Aizu, CodeChef and GeeksforGeeks problems, and 989 Codeforces problems from open-r1/codeforces (Penedo et al., 2025). Problems are admitted with at least 3 tests, a reference solution, and a single accepted answer, since one reference output cannot label a problem with several accepted answers. Stored tests whose inputs violate the constraints of the problem description are removed before use, which drops 1,028 of 90,885 test rows on Codeforces and 2,119 of 22,115 on AtCoder. Difficulty in Table 3 follows the labels of LeetCode and TACO and the ratings of open-r1/codeforces. The 1,484 problems without a label, including all Aizu problems, take the tier that an LLM judge assigns in the conversion audit, where easy problems need direct simulation or a single formula, medium problems a standard technique and hard problems a non-obvious idea or a combination of techniques.

C.2 Problem format

Each Codeforces and AtCoder problem, whose input is given from standard input, is rephrased into a typed function interface and admitted only when the reference solution still passes the stored tests through that interface. Conversion admits 3,490 of the 4,314 Codeforces problems (80.9%). The rejected problems have stored tests that no reference solution reproduces (361), inputs that change under parsing and unparsing (259), several accepted answers (184), or other harness errors (20). Freezing the test cases removes 205 more problems, 201 of which lack 3 invalid inputs for L1b, and leaves 3,285. Of the 1,440 AtCoder problems, conversion admits 892, an audit for descriptions that drop a stated condition and for examples that violate the stated constraints leaves 677, and freezing leaves 623. Most AtCoder rejections at conversion are inputs that change under parsing and unparsing (352 of 548), which trace to faulty stored tests such as leading zeros or counts that do not match the input.

C.3 Data breakdown

We count the samples of each task for supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and AuXSpec-Test (Table 11). A reinforcement learning sample is a generation prompt, and repair prompts are built during training from failed rollouts (Section 4.3).

The 19,492 supervised fine-tuning samples are drawn from the synthesis pipeline of Section 3 and expert iteration (Table 12). An expert-iteration repair chain accepted after more than 1 round becomes 1 generation sample with a reasoning trace over the first attempt, feedback and repair.

The corpus builder also removes samples longer than 16,384 tokens (42), duplicate samples (57), samples beyond 3 per problem and task (11), and 1 sample that is not a whole file.

C.4 Expert iteration details

Each round samples 1 refinement chain per problem and task from a fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. A chain generates an output, compiles the output, and repairs the output for up to 8 rounds, or 16 rounds in the last round of expert iteration. A chain is accepted under the criteria of Section 2, and the reasons of each judge rejection enter the next repair round as review text. Expert iteration runs 3 rounds (Table 13). The first 2 rounds sample from the model fine-tuned on the LeetCode data, and the last round from the model fine-tuned on the data of the first 2 rounds and the Codeforces pipeline data. Accepted chains that pass at the first round become generation samples, and later rounds become repair samples or are rewritten into generation samples (Appendix C.3). A scan over all refinement records adds 384 samples from accepted chains that no round collected. The chains on reinforcement learning problems in the last round add no supervised fine-tuning samples.

Expert iteration adds repairs more than first attempts. Of the 2,268 accepted chains of the LeetCode round, 685 pass at the first round, and of the 298 accepted SpecGen chains on reinforcement learning problems in the last round, 290 need at least 1 repair round.

C.5 Decontamination

The training problems pass filters that remove the 300 AuXSpec-Test problems, the problems that Verina links to, and the reinforcement learning problems from supervised fine-tuning. Verina problems are matched through the LeetCode links in the Verina descriptions, where 43 of the 189 problems link to 36 LeetCode problems. The filters remove 21 samples of AuXSpec-Test problems and 166 samples of 32 LeetCode problems that Verina links to, and a recount of the final training data finds no problem of these sets.

Appendix D Evaluation

D.1 Metrics

Compile@kk and Pass@kk. We follow the standard definition of pass@kk (Chen et al., 2021) and define compile@kk by analogy. For a problem with kk samples, compile@kk is 1 when at least one sample compiles, and pass@kk is 1 when at least one sample meets the acceptance criteria of Section 2. The reported value is the mean over problems, which equals the unbiased estimator of pass@kk (Chen et al., 2021) since exactly kk samples are drawn per problem. Test case alignment compares the test lines of a sample with the frozen test cases regardless of layer headings, and Lean code blocks are extracted regardless of the capitalization of the language tag.

D.2 Token efficiency

We measure output tokens per response and per solved sample (Table 14). AuXSpec-27B-RL requires the fewest output tokens per solved sample of all 13 models in the 4 generation settings. On SpecGen of AuXSpec-Test, it requires 80% fewer tokens per solved sample than GPT-5.6-Sol, the most economical frontier model (2.7K vs. 13.2K), while its pass@1 is 35.9 points higher (65.7% vs. 29.8%; Table 4). RL lowers the cost per solved SpecGen sample at both model sizes, as pass@1 grows faster than the response length (19.3K to 2.7K tokens for the 27B model and 36.0K to 11.0K for the 9B model).

RL changes the length of the reasoning trace in opposite directions at the 2 model sizes. Reasoning traces of the 27B model become shorter after RL, whereas reasoning traces of the 9B model become longer (1.6K to 0.4K and 1.7K to 4.6K thinking tokens per SpecGen response). A plausible reading is that the larger model needs less explicit reasoning to state a specification, whereas the smaller model relies on longer reasoning to reach a correct output. Thinking tokens are the tokens of the thinking segment. Tokens of our models and the backbones are counted with the tokenizer of the backbone, and tokens of the frontier models are the output tokens reported by the API, thinking included.

D.3 General capabilities

To assess general capabilities after specialization, we evaluate the backbones, SFT models and RL models on AIME 25 (Mathematical Association of America, 2025), GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024), and HumanEval+ and MBPP+ of EvalPlus (Liu et al., 2023). EvalPlus extends HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) with more test cases per problem. Sampling follows the settings of DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) with temperature 0.6, top-pp 0.95 and at most 32K output tokens, and pass@1 averages 64 samples per problem on AIME 25, 8 on GPQA-Diamond and 4 on HumanEval+ and MBPP+.

Supervised fine-tuning lowers all 4 scores of both backbones, most on AIME 25, by 36.7 points for the 9B model and 53.1 for the 27B model (Table 15). RL recovers 72% of this drop on AIME 25 at both sizes and about half of the drop on GPQA-Diamond (47% and 52%). On the 2 code benchmarks, AuXSpec-9B-RL surpasses its backbone (88.6% vs. 86.6% on HumanEval+ and 70.8% vs. 65.3% on MBPP+), and AuXSpec-27B-RL trails its backbone by 3.2 and 1.5 points.

D.4 Self-repair on ICPC-Eval

Besides generation, AuXSpec models are trained on the repair tasks (Section 2), which revise a rejected output from compiler and judge feedback. To assess the value of this ability, we evaluate AuXSpec-27B-RL on ICPC-Eval (Xu et al., 2025b), a benchmark of competitive programming problems whose specifications require careful definitions. Of its 118 problems, we exclude 28 problems with multiple correct outputs, which a fixed expected output cannot judge, and 15 problems whose test cases exceed the length range of AuXSpec-Test, which leaves 75 problems. Following Refine@K of ICPC-Eval and the comparison of self-repair with i.i.d. sampling at an equivalent budget (Olausson et al., 2024), we compare 3 settings within a budget of kk model calls per problem:

  • •

    Pass@kk draws kk independent samples and is estimated from 16 samples.

  • •

    Refine@kk with compiler and judge feedback draws 1 sample and returns each rejected output with the compiler messages or the judge findings, in the format of the repair tasks, until an output is accepted or kk calls are made.

  • •

    Refine@kk with compiler feedback only follows the same chain and stops at the first output that compiles.

All settings sample at temperature 0.6 and top-p 0.95 with at most 32,768 generated tokens, and the acceptance criteria (Section 2) score every output.

With compiler and judge feedback, refine@16 reaches 82.7%, compared with 61.3% for pass@16 at an equivalent budget (Figure 3). With compiler feedback only, more chains compile within 2 rounds than independent samples do (88.0% vs. 79.3% for compile@2), but refine@16 reaches 44.0%, as the chain stops at the first output that compiles and the 42 outputs that the judges reject are never revised.

Appendix E Training method analysis

E.1 Expert iteration

SpecGen pass@4 rises at each stage of the SFT data (Table 16), from 30.7% on the LeetCode data to 39.3% after adding the first round of expert iteration and 47.3% after further adding the Codeforces problems and 2 more rounds.

E.2 Continued pretraining

Motivation. An early supervised fine-tuning run of Qwen3.5-9B compiles 5.05% of the 1,208 SpecGen samples and 3.8% of all 3,596 samples on the held-out problems. Classifying the first compiler error of the failed samples shows that 40.8% misuse Mathlib declarations, through application type mismatches (17.3%), invalid fields or projections (14.7%) and type mismatches (8.7%), and 65.2% once unknown identifiers (11.6%) and missing instances (12.8%) are counted. With retrieved declaration names in 58% of the answers, the failures come from the use of Mathlib.

Corpus. Synthesis augments prompts with Mathlib declarations retrieved for the problem (Appendix G.1.2), and across the 3,109 LeetCode problems the retrievals cover 1,381 distinct declarations, of which 1,298 are found in the pinned Mathlib source. These declarations come from 411 files, and we take all declarations of those files rather than the retrieved ones alone, which yields 26,936 declaration heads. The heads are rewritten with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) into English lessons that state the content, the application, the occasion and the contrast of a declaration, which follows the rewriting of raw corpora into reading-comprehension text (Cheng et al., 2024) and textbook-style synthetic corpora (Gunasekar et al., 2023). Together with 8,312 rows of Mathlib source, 2,336 lessons on decidability routes and 3,790 pairs of compiler error and repair, the corpus ℳ\mathcal{M} holds 41,374 rows and about 43M tokens.

Training and result. Adding problems to supervised fine-tuning improves pass@4 more than continued pretraining does (Table 17). Continued pretraining minimizes the next-token loss on the corpus,

ℒCPT(θ)=−𝔼u∼ℳ∑tlogπθ(ut∣u<t),\mathcal{L}_{\text{CPT}}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{u\sim\mathcal{M}}\sum_{t}\log\pi_{\theta}(u_{t}\mid u_{<t}), (3)

for 2 epochs, 92 steps, on Qwen3.5-9B base with learning rate 5e-6 and sequence length 16,384, and supervised fine-tuning follows on 4,826 rows from 1,631 problems. Domain corpora of this kind help on downstream tasks (Gururangan et al., 2020) and formal provers are pretrained on Lean and mathematics before fine-tuning (Azerbayev et al., 2024; Xin et al., 2025), yet the benefit of continued pretraining is not universal (Shi & Lipani, 2023). Here continued pretraining improves SpecGen pass@4 from 8.2 to 9.8 and pass@4 over the 4 tasks from 26.4 to 27.4, whereas adding 1,056 problems, 3,167 rows, to supervised fine-tuning improves the same 2 numbers to 13.7 and 30.2. The corpus loss falls from 1.03 to 0.69 with held-out perplexity 2.03. The corpus is therefore fit while the downstream gain stays at 1.0 point, the distance between document perplexity and downstream use reported for knowledge injection through continued pretraining (Jiang et al., 2024). Content memorized from a corpus becomes usable after many representations of the same content (Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024; Yang et al., 2025), and each of the 26,936 declarations appears in 1 lesson here. Lessons state the meaning of declarations, whereas a compiling specification requires declarations composed into terms that the elaborator accepts, and added problems carry test cases and judges that label samples of that composition. Later rounds therefore put the effort into data.

E.3 Reinforcement learning

The final recipe for AuXSpec-9B-RL and AuXSpec-27B-RL combines the progressive reward of Eq. (1), the self-repair buffer, the overlong penalty and the mask on repetitive rollouts on the clipped surrogate of DAPO with batch-normalized advantages (Section 4.3), and adds the end-of-sequence penalty for the 27B model. The runs on the 9B model develop the recipe, and both models train for 1 epoch, 434 steps for the 9B model and 208 steps for the 27B model, with the settings of Table 9. Both runs remain stable through the epoch, with 0.12% and 0.60% of rollouts repetitive and 0.13% and 0.11% malformed for the 27B and 9B models. The reported models are the final checkpoints, and SpecGen pass@1 on AuXSpec-Test still rises over the last evaluated checkpoints, from 54.3% at step 400 to 58.6% for the 9B model and from 61.3% at step 200 to 65.7% for the 27B model. The subsections below analyze the reward stages, the reward dynamics and pass@kk.

E.3.1 Reward stages

The progressive reward keeps most groups without a passing rollout in the gradient. Under a binary reward these groups have equal rewards and are discarded by dynamic sampling (Yu et al., 2025). They make up 37% of SpecGen groups for the 27B model and 47% for the 9B model, and the progressive reward keeps nonzero variance in 87.9% and 86.2% of them (Table 18).

Table 19 lists the reward and the fraction of rollouts of each outcome. Each rule against reward hacking closes a shortcut that the stages would otherwise reward. A test that calls no declaration of the output, such as #guard true, passes without testing the output, and counting only tests that call a declaration keeps the test stages meaningful. An escape hatch, the sorry and admit tactics, an axiom declaration or the native_decide tactic, lets an output compile without the checks that later stages assume. Special-casing the test inputs, excluding a test value from the validity predicate and copying the given test cases into the implementation all pass the test stages without solving the problem and receive 0. Altering a given test case lets a rollout pass the test stages against a different expected output and receives 0.1. A test that cannot run would otherwise earn the test execution credit of a test that ran and failed. An unchanged repair would keep the credit of the stages the failed input already passes. The non-tautology stage precedes the overall quality stage, the order in which evaluation runs the judges.

The partial credit separates accepted outputs by form. The non-tautology judge classifies a specification as declarative, enumerative or tautological. A declarative specification states the condition of the problem and is sound and complete: every answer that satisfies the specification is correct, and every correct answer satisfies the specification. An enumerative specification states the same condition over a candidate list that the specification constructs, such as all sublists of the input, instead of quantifying over the candidate type. A tautological specification replaces the condition with an algorithm for the answer, which is the role of the implementation. The implementation judge marks a correct CodeGen implementation as slow when the implementation takes more than about 10710^{7} steps on the largest admitted input and a method faster by more than a logarithmic factor exists, known as a slow positive (Li et al., 2022). Appendix K.3 lists both prompts.

As training proceeds, compilation failures fall from 49.0% of rollouts in the first 40 steps to 15.5% in the last 40 steps for the 27B model and from 66.0% to 10.7% for the 9B model, while passing rollouts rise from 18.4% to 45.0% and from 9.9% to 38.5% (Figure 2c and 2d).

E.3.2 Reward dynamics

We analyze the group-relative advantage (Shao et al., 2024) before batch normalization. Replaying the training rollouts with the value of one outcome changed shows how the value sets this advantage (Figure 4a1 and 4a2). Failures that attempt to score unfaithfully are shortcuts rather than progress. For instance, tautological specifications restate algorithms instead of specifying problems, and failed test case alignments usually rewrite the given test cases. Such unfaithful attempts should be discouraged in every group. Higher values, though well below the full reward of 1, still assign these failures positive advantages in groups without correct rollouts, whereas replaying at 0.1 shows advantages that are negative and below those of faithful attempts in almost every group (Table 20).

Based on observation, some attempts make partial progress that is correct in substance but not yet in the perfect form. For instance, 1) enumerative specifications already state the correct condition and only need to be rewritten declaratively, and 2) slow implementations are already correct and only need faster algorithms. Binary judges also classify enumerative specifications poorly. An intermediate reward for partial progress refines sparse signals into fine-grained rewards. When rewards are low, like SpecGen in the early steps, partial progress rewards small improvements of failing attempts, while once correct rollouts are common, declarative specifications and fast implementations are assigned higher advantages.

By replaying the rollouts, we fix intermediate values at which partial progress receives positive advantages in groups with few correct rollouts and negative ones in groups with many. A slow implementation at 0.5 turns negative from 2 passing rollouts of 16, compared with 6 at 0.8, and an enumerative specification at 0.4 turns negative from 3, compared with 14 when valued like a full-score answer. As the policy improves, the advantage of partial progress turns from positive to negative (Figure 4b2 and 4c2). CodeGen groups without a passing rollout fall from 44% in steps 1 to 40 to 0% in steps 161 to 208, and the mean advantage of slow implementations falls from +0.10+0.10 to −0.17-0.17 over the same periods. SpecGen keeps 29% to 52% of groups without a passing rollout in each period, where quality rejections keep a mean advantage near 0 with both signs (Figure 4c1). Partial progress thus provides intermediate supervision that keeps the reward informative throughout training (Table 21).

Whether a partial value acts as credit depends heavily on the capability of the policy to sample better rollouts in the same group. For the 9B model, 71.7% of correct but slow CodeGen rollouts fall in groups without a fast correct rollout, where the slow value keeps a positive advantage, compared with 48.4% for the 27B model, and the 9B run does not start repair rounds from slow rollouts. CodeGen pass@1 of AuXSpec-9B-RL accordingly drops from 77.1% to 44.7% when slow programs count as failures, compared with 94.8% to 88.0% for AuXSpec-27B-RL.

E.3.3 Pass@kk

A key question for RL with verifiable rewards is whether it expands the set of problems a model can solve or only raises the probability of solutions that the starting model already samples. Pass@kk at large kk separates the two, since a starting model that catches up at large kk solves the same problems with more samples (Yue et al., 2025). Prolonged RL has been reported to expand the set most where the starting model is weak (Liu et al., 2025).

We compare AuXSpec-27B-RL with AuXSpec-27B-SFT, the starting model of RL, at temperature 0.6 and top-pp 0.95. Pass@kk follows the unbiased estimator (Chen et al., 2021) on 64 samples per problem for the SFT model and 32 for the RL model. Pass@64, pass@128 and pass@256 count a problem as solved when any of 64, 128 or 256 samples passes, and additional samples are drawn only for problems not yet solved.

The RL model stays above the SFT model at every kk and reaches 96.3%, compared with 85.7% at k=256k=256, where the SFT model remains below the pass@8 of the RL model (88.2%, Figure 5). The SFT model still gains at k=256k=256, while the gain per doubling of kk falls from 5.8 points at k=64k=64 to 4.3 and 2.7 points at k=128k=128 and k=256k=256. The gap narrows from 13.0 to 10.6 points between k=128k=128 and k=256k=256 as the RL model approaches the ceiling, with 11 unsolved problems of which 10 are solved by neither model.

As a result, 33 problems are solved only by the RL model and 1 only by the SFT model within 256 samples (Table 22).

Appendix E.4 reports RL with a distillation term from AuXSpec-27B-SFT.

E.4 On-policy distillation

To transfer the capability of AuXSpec-27B-SFT, the strongest of our models on AuXSpec-Test, to the smaller AuXSpec-9B-SFT, we apply on-policy distillation (OPD) and OPD within reinforcement learning (Agarwal et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a), but neither improves the student model. OPD, with the k3 estimator in the advantage, suffers from mode collapse, where the student model concentrates on the decidable form of the executable postcondition, leading to a compile rate of 2.0% without compiler feedback. SpecGen pass@4 drops from 24.3 to 5.3 while CodeGen changes by at most 3 points. Distillation within reinforcement learning suffers from teacher redundancy, where a teacher model fine-tuned on the same data carries 4% to 7% of the advantage with little information about which samples succeed. We next describe the setup, the failure patterns and the attribution.

Setup. On-policy distillation trains student models on self-generated responses with token-level supervision from teacher models (Agarwal et al., 2024). We select AuXSpec-27B-SFT as the teacher model πT\pi_{T}, the strongest of our models on AuXSpec-Test (Table 4), and AuXSpec-9B-SFT as the student model πθ\pi_{\theta}, which has the same vocabulary and chat template as the teacher model for a locally served teacher model to score student tokens. For a prompt xx and a response y∼πθ(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), the per-token log-ratio

ℓt=log⁡πθ​(yt∣x,y<t)−log⁡πT​(yt∣x,y<t)\ell_{t}=\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})-\log\pi_{T}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}) (4)

is the k1 estimate of the reverse KL divergence KL(πθ∥πT)\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{\theta}\,\|\,\pi_{T}), and k3​(t)=e−ℓt−1+ℓtk_{3}(t)=e^{-\ell_{t}}-1+\ell_{t} is a nonnegative estimate of the same divergence (Schulman, 2020). Both settings enter the policy gradient through the per-token advantage AtA_{t}.

  • •

    OPD: the per-token advantage is At=−k3​(t)A_{t}=-k_{3}(t) with no task reward, as in on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024; Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025), over 200 steps on 12,791 prompts (1 epoch), with student responses and teacher log-probabilities at temperature 1.0.

  • •

    OPD within RL: the objective adds a distillation term with per-token advantage −ℓt-\ell_{t}, weighted by β=0.1\beta=0.1, to the reinforcement learning objective of Appendix E.3, as in joint distillation and reinforcement learning (Xu et al., 2025a) with the k1 estimator in place of k2. Variants keep the distillation term only where the sign agrees with the task advantage (Lin et al., 2026) or drop the term and reweight the task advantage by clipped teacher ratios (Wang et al., 2026a). Student responses are sampled at temperature 0.7 and teacher log-probabilities at 1.0.

Diagnostics. Besides pass@kk, we track token entropy, the fraction of generated text inside repetition loops, the fraction of SpecGen samples in the decidable form of Section 3.1, and teacher informativeness, the mean of −ℓt-\ell_{t} on sequences with positive task advantage minus the same mean on sequences with negative advantage (Wang et al., 2026b).

Results. OPD degrades SpecGen and changes CodeGen by at most 3 points (Table 23). SpecGen pass@4 drops from 24.3 to 5.3 on AuXSpec-Test and from 42.0 to 18.5 on Verina advanced problems, and CodeGen pass@4 from 30.7 to 27.7. In OPD within RL, teacher informativeness stays at +0.004 or below and the teacher term carries 4% to 7% of the total advantage over the first steps. The 3 runs ended at steps 4 to 9 when the judge service ran out of budget, and the measured informativeness led us to stop this line rather than resume.

Phenomena. After OPD, 1,147 of 1,200 SpecGen samples (95.6%) fail at compilation, compared with 1,032 (86.0%) before OPD and 875 (72.9%) for the teacher (Figure 6), and OPD also narrows the sample distribution and lets repetition loops grow unpenalized.

Template concentration. The number of SpecGen samples stating the executable postcondition in the decidable form increases from 150 (12.5%) before OPD to 706 of 1,200 (58.8%) after OPD, compared with 114 (9.5%) for the teacher (Figure 7). Within this form, the compile rate falls from 10.7% to 2.0%, compared with 21.9% for the teacher, and failed samples report a missing decidability instance.

Diversity collapse. Token entropy falls from 0.451 to 0.012 (−-97.3%) within the first 100 steps (Figure 9), the entropy collapse also reported for reinforcement learning (Yu et al., 2025; He et al., 2025). Near-duplicate sample pairs occur on 40.7% of SpecGen problems, compared with 0.3% before OPD (Figure 8). On Verina basic problems, pass@1 rises from 39.8 to 44.7 while pass@4 falls from 75.9 to 63.0, the pattern of diversity collapse in which gains at small kk are paired with losses at larger kk (Dang et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2025).

Degenerate agreement. Repetition loops (Holtzman et al., 2020) grow during training, and from step 51 on, looping responses hold 43% to 51% of the generated text. Inside a loop, the teacher ranks the next student token first on 98.9% of tokens, compared with 90.7% before the loop, and the k3 loss per token therefore drops from 0.136 to 0.019 (−-86.0%, Figure 10). The same degenerate agreement is reported for on-policy distillation (Yu et al., 2026). Loops account for 1 of the 60 SpecGen problems lost to OPD, where all 4 samples are truncated or loop.

Attribution. We attribute the SpecGen drop to estimator bias, which lowers entropy throughout training, to mode collapse, which moves probability onto a form that often fails to compile, and to teacher redundancy, which makes the teacher term uninformative about sample success.

  1. 1.

    Estimator bias. With k3k_{3} inside the advantage, the policy gradient is a biased estimate of the reverse KL gradient that also raises the forward KL, and this configuration is reported to collapse training (Shah et al., 2026). The entropy decline of Figure 9 matches this bias.

  2. 2.

    Mode collapse. The pipeline sets the decidable form as the first executable postcondition and replaces the form through instance synthesis or a separate definition when compilation fails (Section 3.1), and the form covers 35.5% of synthesized problems as a result. Evaluation scores single samples without compiler feedback. We conjecture that the mode-seeking reverse KL (Agarwal et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2026) moves probability onto this frequent form, including on problems where the form does not compile. The student adopts the form in 54.6% of samples on problems where the teacher never adopts it. OPD therefore amplifies the form beyond teacher usage.

  3. 3.

    Teacher redundancy. Teacher models with higher scores help only when offering capabilities beyond the experience of the student (Li et al., 2026a). Teacher and student are fine-tuned on the same data, and although OPD within RL adds the fine-grained reward of reinforcement learning, the teacher term stays uninformative about which samples succeed.

Identical tokenizers and chat templates rule out a format mismatch, and on problems the teacher fails, the student stops at the failing stage of the teacher no more often after OPD than before.

Appendix F Ablation study

F.1 Shared backbone with VeriSpecGen

To compare with VeriSpecGen on a shared backbone, we fix the backbone to Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, the backbone of VeriSpecGen-4B, and keep the rest of our pipeline: the same SFT data and configuration (19,492 samples, 3 epochs), the RL recipe of AuXSpec-27B (Section 4.3; 64 problems and 16 samples per step), and the same evaluation protocol (Section 5.3), with the official Verina evaluator at temperature 0.3.

With our prompts and acceptance criteria, the backbone before training scores 0.0% SpecGen pass@1 on both AuXSpec-Test and Verina (Tables 24 and 25). None of its 1,200 SpecGen samples on AuXSpec-Test compiles: the outputs either reach the generation length limit or contain Lean errors such as Lean 3 syntax. VeriSpecGen reports 14.7% for the same backbone with its own prompt and evaluation harness, so the 2 base rows are not directly comparable.

SFT on our data improves generation only slightly (6.9% SpecGen pass@1 on Verina without test cases, close to 9.5% for VeriSpecGen-4B SFT Spec-Only), while the repair tasks improve the most (from 6.5% to 49.0% SpecGen-Repair pass@1 on AuXSpec-Test).

RL accounts for most of the gain. On Verina without test cases, SpecGen pass@1 improves by about 6 points every 20 steps, from 23.0% at step 20 to 54.2% at step 120, and still improves by 3.5 points between steps 100 and 120 (Table 25). From step 40, all 4 scores surpass every VeriSpecGen-4B model, and from step 100 every VeriSpecGen model including the 30B-A3B models (54.2% and 77.2% SpecGen and CodeGen pass@1 at step 120, compared with at most 47.6% and 61.2%), where our pass@4 is compared with their pass@10. On AuXSpec-Test, SpecGen pass@1 improves from 1.2% after SFT to 24.0% at step 120 and CodeGen pass@1 from 7.2% to 57.8%, and both still rise (Table 24). Our SFT data contain 19,492 samples, compared with 121,531 (No-Test) or 343,827 (Full) examples for the VeriSpecGen models.

F.2 RL recipe ablation

To isolate the contribution of each component, we construct 3 variants of the RL recipe of AuXSpec-9B, each removing one component, and train them from AuXSpec-9B-SFT with the same training prompts, order and seed:

  • •

    w/o test execution compiles each rollout without its test cases, so no test case is executed, and keeps all judge stages.

  • •

    w/o LLM judges assigns the top reward to every rollout that passes the test cases.

  • •

    w/o self-repair fills every batch slot with a new training prompt.

The variant without self-repair therefore consumes training prompts faster, so each variant is compared with AuXSpec-9B-RL after approximately the same number of training prompts rather than at the same step (Table 26). Evaluation follows Table 4.

LLM judges. Without LLM judges in the reward, the model exploits the reward by restating the given test cases as the specification. We note that the training reward keeps increasing, while SpecGen pass@1 on AuXSpec-Test reaches its highest value around step 100 and then decreases (Figure 11c1). The gap between the 2 therefore widens over training (84.7% of SpecGen rollouts accepted in steps 141–150 vs. 20.0% pass@1 at step 150, down from 35.8% at step 100). Tautological specifications account for a growing part of the evaluation samples (1.9% at step 50 vs. 58.8% at step 150). On Verina, these specifications pass the test cases given in the prompt but fail without them (88.4% vs. 52.0% SpecGen pass@1 at step 150).

Test execution. Without test execution in the reward, the reward accepts implementations that the test cases would reject. About half of the CodeGen rollouts pass the remaining stages early in training (49.7% vs. 19.7% of CodeGen rollouts accepted in steps 41–50 without and with test execution), while CodeGen pass@1 on AuXSpec-Test improves slowly (Figure 11b2). After approximately the same number of training prompts the variant falls behind AuXSpec-9B-RL in both tasks (34.4% vs. 65.0% CodeGen and 24.3% vs. 34.9% SpecGen pass@1 after 4,111 and 4,162 prompts). The gap in CodeGen persists at step 150 even though the variant has drawn more training prompts (37.6% vs. 65.0% after 4,796 vs. 4,162 prompts; Table 26). Repair remains comparable to the other runs (65.8% SpecGen-Repair pass@1 at step 150), so the variant falls behind in generating a correct output from scratch. The judges alone cannot check the behavior of an implementation, and test execution keeps the reward accurate.

Self-repair. Without self-repair every batch slot holds a new training prompt. The variant therefore consumes training prompts faster and outperforms AuXSpec-9B-RL at the same step (43.1% vs. 34.9% SpecGen pass@1 at steps 150 and 140 after 6,334 vs. 4,162 prompts). AuXSpec-9B-RL outperforms it in both generation and repair even after fewer training prompts (21.8% vs. 14.7% SpecGen and 54.3% vs. 45.8% SpecGen-Repair pass@1 after 2,149 and 2,396 prompts). After about 6.2K prompts it still outperforms the variant in generation (46.7% vs. 43.1% SpecGen pass@1; Table 26). Training without repair tasks is thus a viable recipe when new problems are plentiful.

The repair tasks are designed for settings in which a model revises its output from feedback over several rounds, such as long-horizon verification and collaboration between agents. Refinement from compiler and judge feedback is part of the training objective, and the model also refines its specifications at test time: on ICPC-Eval, refine@16 reaches 82.7% of the problems, compared with 61.3% for pass@16 (Appendix D.4).

We also report Verina at the same checkpoints, where the variants follow similar trends (Table 27).

Appendix G Pipeline details

Figure 12 shows the pipeline of Figure 1 on a running example, with the input of each stage and the Lean code that the stage produces. Each stage below ends with an analysis of the stage on the 3,037 synthesized problems.

G.1 Preprocessing

G.1.1 Test cases

For each of 3,109 problems (719 easy, 1,622 medium, 768 hard), we screen the stored examples and propose negative test cases, invalid inputs and incorrect outputs beside the positive test cases. Invalid inputs are proposed by category (a value just outside a stated bound, a size outside the stated range, a container of the wrong shape, a broken structural invariant, parameters invalid only together, a value outside the stated domain), and incorrect outputs by category (a near miss, a suboptimal feasible answer, an unattainable answer, the answer under a relaxed constraint, an output of the wrong shape, a degenerate answer). Benchmarks store negative test cases beside positive ones (Ye et al., 2026a; Ye et al., 2026b), since a specification that accepts correct outputs on the given examples can still accept incorrect outputs (Endres et al., 2024).

A proposed incorrect output is admitted when the reference solution, run on the proposed valid input, returns an output that is not a reordering of the proposed output. Invalid inputs are proposed together with the violated constraint and are dropped on coinciding with a valid example of the problem. Cases too large for compiled evaluation and cases whose stored answer is null are refused before any model call, with the measured thresholds in Appendix G.5.

The 27,981 test cases, 9 per problem, are assembled into 18 #guard commands per problem, one per test case and layer of Table 7, with each positive test case reused at L1a, L2a, L3, and L4. A #guard command runs compiled code, and a passed test case relies on the compiler and runtime as trusted base, the same as native_decide. For the test cases, we store the provenance (public example or synthesized) and the admission round. A test case judged wrong is replaced by a held-back test case at most once per problem.

Analysis. The frozen test cases, negative test cases included, are shown to the generation model, and the negative test cases act as part of the problem statement rather than as a hidden filter. Of 3,276 specification candidates tested at L1a and L1b, 8 (0.24%) fail only at L1b, and of 3,195 executable postconditions tested at L2a and L2b, 4 (0.13%) fail only at L2b. The 4 failures at L2b have one cause, a lossy output decoder in the specification, such as a tree decoder that drops children below null nodes. The 8 failures at L1b fall on 5 problems, and in 4 of the 5 problems the frozen invalid input is in fact valid. Repair narrowed the precondition to reject that input in all 5 problems. Frozen test values keep test cases from adapting to a wrong specification, and these 5 preconditions are the only adaptation in the opposite direction.

Screening. Before any model call, test cases are filtered by size and by null answers. A test case containing a list or string longer than 128 items is refused, since a case is frozen as a literal that compiled evaluation builds item by item. We cap compilation at 600 seconds on the Lean server and observe that a test case exceeding the cap terminates the serving REPL. The threshold was measured over the stored test cases, and any threshold between 102 and 185 items refuses the same test cases. A case whose stored answer is null is refused in the layers that read an answer, since the source dataset stores null wherever the answer is a mutated argument, and a null true answer makes each negative built from the null answer meaningless.

G.1.2 Library retrieval

Models reference library declarations absent from the pinned library version (Chakraborty et al., 2025). Typed queries against Mathlib, for a definition, a theorem, or an instance, are generated together with one sentence stating the use the specification has for the answer, and relevance is judged against that sentence. Search candidates are deduplicated, elaborated with #check against the pinned toolchain, and judged for relevance by an LLM given the problem description. Specification synthesis is augmented with the declarations admitted by the relevance judge, 4.2 per problem, each with a checked signature and a one-sentence reason from the LLM. Appendix G.5 reports the counts at each step.

Analysis. Elaboration keeps declarations that exist only in newer Mathlib versions out of specification synthesis (Table 28). 23,608 queries (14,888 definition, 5,052 theorem, 3,668 instance) produced 92,104 candidates. Of the elaborated declarations, 5.4% were absent from the pinned Mathlib, and review dropped 10.0% of the reviewed candidates. Of the 13,191 stored declarations, specification synthesis of the 3,037 problems received 12,876, 4.2 per problem, with 131 problems receiving none. The absent declarations originate in a search index built on the latest Mathlib, while synthesis compiles against the pinned version. Retrieved declarations do not change the first compilation. Specifications that reference a retrieved declaration by the full name compile at the first attempt in 83.2% of 1,871 problems, and the other specifications in 83.9% of 1,032.

G.2 Specifications

Planning. A type plan fixes the declaration names and one type per parameter, with a conversion function wherever the stored value has a different type. The postcondition is then planned regardless of decidability, which keeps computation out of the postcondition. A frozen test value is printed once as the expression used by all test layers to prevent models from altering the value.

Formalization.

Each component is generated separately and compiled with the accepted components. The #guard commands of the layers are generated from the expressions the plan fixed, and each command is accepted at the first passing check in the order shape, verbatim expression, token-level expression, and judge review of equivalence. The shape check admits one command per test case, attached to the declaration of that layer and with the polarity of the test case. The expression check compares the tokens of the printed expression, which keeps whitespace from merging 2 values.

Executable postcondition. The executable postcondition is first set to the decidable form of the postcondition, and the file is compiled. When no decidability instance is derived, a model supplies instances from the compiler diagnostics for up to 3 rounds. When the supplied instances still fail to elaborate, a separate definition is generated. Only a separate definition can disagree with the postcondition, which the L2a and L2b test cases detect on the tested outputs and the postcondition equivalence theorem excludes on all valid inputs. Appendix G.5 reports the counts by form.

Judges. The postcondition judge is given the problem description, the constraints, and the postcondition source. A rejection quotes a sentence of the description and names an output that the postcondition admits and the problem excludes. The executable postcondition judge is given the constraints, the accepted precondition and postcondition, and the executable postcondition, and a rejection names a valid input with a witness or counterexample that the executable postcondition misses or wrongly admits. The tautology judge rejects a postcondition that computes the output. Problems whose natural statement is the transformation itself are labeled in advance by a majority vote of 3 classifier calls, and the label exempts the problem from the tautology judge. The rejected component is repaired with the named error, or replanned for an error in the plan.

G.2.1 Example problems

Separate executable postcondition.

We illustrate the format with problem 1955 Count Number of Special Subsequences from AuXSpec-Test (Figures 13 and 15a). In this problem, we are given an array over {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\} and need to count, modulo 109+710^{9}+7, the subsequences of the form 0a​1b​2c0^{a}1^{b}2^{c} with a,b,c≥1a,b,c\geq 1. The postcondition states the result as the size of the set of index sets whose selected elements take this form. The executable postcondition enumerates all subsets of the indices, a brute-force computation that finishes on the short test inputs. The implementation counts in 1 pass with 3 counters, for subsequences of 0s, of 0s followed by 1s, and of 0s, 1s and 2s, since an element either extends or skips the subsequences counted so far. Since neither specification mentions the counters, the correctness theorem relates the recurrence to the set of index sets.

For this problem, a natural postcondition characterizes the valid index sets SS as exactly those that select a subsequence of the form 0+​1+​2+0^{+}1^{+}2^{+} from the input. This characterization is not directly executable, since it ranges over arbitrary finite sets of natural numbers. However, every relevant index set is contained in the input indices. The executable postcondition therefore enumerates 2{0,…,input.length−1}2^{\{0,\ldots,\text{input.length}-1\}} and counts the subsets satisfying the same property. The two formulations describe the same relation but are not definitionally identical in Lean, so the postcondition equivalence theorem connects the logical characterization with the bounded enumeration.

Executable postcondition through type class resolution.

We illustrate the decidable form with problem 523 Continuous Subarray Sum from AuXSpec-Test (Figures 15a, 16 and 16). In this problem, we are given an array of non-negative integers and a positive integer kk and need to decide whether some contiguous subarray of length at least 2 sums to a multiple of kk. The postcondition states that the result is true exactly when there exist 2 indices and an integer multiplier nn such that the subarray between the indices sums to n⋅kn\cdot k.

The executable postcondition applies decide to the postcondition, which compiles only when type class resolution finds a Decidable instance for the unfolded proposition. The existential over natural-number indices and an integer multiplier has no such instance as stated, since the quantifiers range over unbounded domains. The pipeline therefore synthesizes a type class instance that bounds both indices by the length of the array, replaces the multiplier by integer divisibility, and proves the bounded proposition equivalent to the original with decidable_of_iff. Type class resolution then assembles the executable postcondition from this instance and the library instances for bounded quantifiers and divisibility, so the executable postcondition agrees with the postcondition by construction (Appendix H.2). The implementation, omitted from the figure, scans prefix sums modulo kk with a map from each remainder to the earliest prefix index at which the remainder occurs, and the correctness theorem relates this scan to the existential of the postcondition.

G.2.2 Analysis

The specification judges rarely reject, and the errors that pass all checks are in the meaning of the specification. Each verdict in Table 29 corresponds to a distinct component that compiles and passes the test layers of the component. The specification judges reject 1.7% to 3.8% of the verdicts, and all rejected problems are accepted after repair. The errors that proving or human review later found had all passed the test layers and the judge of the erroneous component. In 2 problems a correct rejection led to a repair that introduced the error found by review, and in 1 problem the judge accepted on a second reading the defect that the judge had named.

The decidable form is reliable where the postcondition quantifies over bounded types (Figure 17). The decidable form serves 1,079 of the 3,037 problems (35.5%). Of the other 1,958 problems, 1,343 have postconditions that quantify over unbounded types, 319 were synthesized before instance synthesis was added, 287 fail instance synthesis for 3 rounds, 6 remain unexplained, and 3 are routed to the decidable form but keep a separate definition in the final file. Where the decidable form applies, the executable postcondition passes all checks at the first attempt in 772 of 787 problems (98.1%), compared with 1,178 of 2,250 (52.4%) for separately generated executable postconditions. Missing instances arise from the decidable form. The pipeline first sets the executable postcondition to decide applied to the postcondition, which compiles only when Lean finds a decidability instance for the postcondition. A postcondition that quantifies over an unbounded type (e.g., over all natural numbers or all lists) has no computable instance as stated, and instance synthesis fails, for example on add-digits, where no decidability instance can be synthesized for a postcondition that quantifies over all digit roots dd.

G.3 Implementation

Implementation planning is given the accepted specification as read-only text and selects an algorithm with cost argument, listing specification definitions to call and definitions to replace with reason. The plan is checked before generation for a termination argument based on a decreasing quantity of the input, a stated cost consistent with the approach and the input bounds, a replacement justified by cost or by a different question, and an algorithm that computes the answer, without search over candidates. Beyond the properties in Section 3.1, the implementation judge reports computations already available in the specification.

G.3.1 Analysis

Test cases on small inputs admit false positives (Li et al., 2022), and the implementation judge rejects 717 of the 3,667 implementations (19.6%) that pass all test cases (Figure 18).

  • •

    Fuel parameters (270). The implementation recurses on a fuel argument, which hides nontermination on inputs beyond the test cases.

  • •

    Cost beyond the input bounds (234). The implementation is correct but exceeds the cost that the stated input bounds allow, known as a slow positive (Li et al., 2022).

  • •

    Restated executable postconditions (198). The implementation repeats a computation of the executable postcondition that already runs within the stated input bounds.

  • •

    Replayed test cases (15). The implementation returns stored outputs for the tested inputs.

The implementation judge is waived after 2 retries, and 133 problems keep an implementation that the judge rejected. Of these, 89 are rejected for a fuel argument that may hide nontermination, 27 for cost beyond the input bounds, 12 for restating the executable postcondition and 5 for replaying test cases. 12 of the 133 are in AuXSpec-Test, and for the 9 among them rejected for fuel, the correctness proofs show that the fuel suffices on all valid inputs.

G.4 Repair

Compilation runs through the Kimina Lean server (Santos et al., 2025), a REPL-based server (Lean community, 2023). Repair revises rejected components separately for at most 18 rounds per run of the repair loop, which a problem re-enters after replanning. From the second round on, the repair input includes a digest of earlier attempts, and a root-cause analysis runs for errors that line numbers cannot attribute. Repair stops early when a revision repeats an earlier diff or does not change the component. Where a repair attributes the error to a test case, the attribution is reviewed by a judge, and a confirmed attribution replaces the test case with a held-back test case at most once per problem.

G.4.1 Analysis

Repair recovers most first failures within 2 rounds (Figure 19). The fraction of the 3,037 problems accepted within kk repair rounds rises from 78.1% at k=0k=0 to 93.9% at k=1k=1 and 97.5% at k=2k=2 for the postcondition, from 67.7% to 91.9% and 97.7% for the executable postcondition, and from 64.3% to 85.0% and 94.4% for the implementation.

The remaining problems took 1,030 postcondition repair rounds, 1,321 executable postcondition rounds and 1,842 implementation rounds (Figure 20).

1,081 problems (34.8% of the 3,109 seeds) need no repair round for any component, and repair recovers most of the others, most on hard problems, where 22.1% of the seeds pass without repair and 95.7% with repair (Figure 21).

Repair never replaces a frozen test case. Repair attributed 113 failures on 96 problems to test cases, and the root-cause analyzer placed the fault in the model-generated #guard command in 55 and in the plan in 52, never in a frozen test case. The most frequent case is a negative test case with a negative value for an input that the plan types as a natural number, which the judge resolves by changing the planned type to an integer. Repair rounds go to Lean usage rather than to failed test cases (Figure 22). Of 3,852 recorded rounds, Mathlib API errors take 29.7%, missing instances 23.8% (Appendix G.2.2), type mismatches 12.6%, parse errors 11.3%, proof obligations 10.0%, and failed test cases 3.1%. The fraction of Mathlib API errors matches the misuse of Mathlib declarations that motivates continued pretraining (Appendix E.2).

G.5 Outcomes

We break down the outcomes of Section 3.2 by difficulty (Table 30).

The decidable form of the postcondition is adopted in 1,079 problems (35.5%) and a separate definition in 1,958 problems. The frozen #guard commands of 90.0% of the synthesized problems match the planned expressions verbatim, and the other 303 needed token-level matching or a judge.

G.6 Training samples

The reasoning trace of a training sample is rephrased from the reasoning recorded while that problem was synthesized, which is the planning and generation reasoning for the generation tasks and the diagnostics, root cause, and repair reasoning for the repair tasks. A rephrased trace is admitted only when each sentence is grounded in the recorded reasoning, the answer is not stated before being derived, and no pipeline vocabulary appears.

G.7 Cost

Synthesis and supporting experiments cost $2,604 over 226,351 model calls, divided across 9 accounts (Table 31). Accounts follow record keeping, and reasoning-trace rephrasing, model comparisons, and discarded experiments are listed beside retrieval, test case construction, and formalization. Accounts cover different problems, and per-problem costs are not compared across accounts.

Of the 7 accounts with recorded tokens, some are the provider-reported per-call charge as recorded by the pipeline, and the rest are priced from the recorded tokens at the list rate of the provider. The other 2 accounts are estimated from their call counts. List pricing ignores the lower rate for cached input and therefore overstates the cost of the priced accounts. The table lists the models of the accounts, since an account mixes the prices of several models.

The remaining 2 accounts, classification and judging, have a call count and no dollars. One vote is one call in both, and the 99,736 calls are therefore exact. Both accounts recorded calls without tokens and are counted by calls, outside the dollar total.

The dollars and the tokens of the formalization row count different calls. 6,237 of the formalization calls were served from the response cache, at no charge, and these calls make up 12.0% of the tokens in the formalization account. Since tokens include cached calls and dollars exclude cached calls, dollars per token understate the price.

Formalization is the largest account at $2,024, which is $0.65 per problem on average, $0.47 at the median, and $6.68 at the maximum. A median problem took 17 calls and 23 minutes wall clock, and thinking tokens account for 91.9% of the 290M output tokens of the formalization account.

Table 32 breaks the formalization calls down by role, where a call type averaging below one call per problem is skipped on some problems, when an earlier check settles the decision or when the corresponding stage does not run.

The total is a lower bound, since runs discarded during development left no record. Since cached runs record the tokens of the original calls, successful runs are fully counted.

G.8 Model selection

Frontier models are compared separately for generation and repair, implementation planning, and judging. The candidates are Kimi-K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), GLM-5.2 (Z.ai, 2026), Claude-Opus-5 (Anthropic, 2026a), and Claude-Sonnet-5 (Anthropic, 2026b).

G.8.1 Formalizer

The comparison of generation models replaces the model for the 7 calls that generate or repair definitions and #guard commands, and keeps all other calls fixed. Four calls generate the postcondition, the executable postcondition, the implementation, and the #guard commands, and 3 repair these components from compiler diagnostics. Each configuration is run with a separate response cache to keep replies from being replayed across configurations, and pass rate, repair rounds, token count, cost, and wall-clock time in Table 33 are measured on fresh calls.

Three candidates formalize all 30 problems and are separated by efficiency (Table 33). Claude-Opus-5 repairs least and still costs the most per problem. DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash are the cheapest but formalize 2 fewer problems and take the longest, and wall-clock time limits throughput since each repair round occupies a compilation process. Kimi-K3 formalizes all problems at lower cost than Claude-Opus-5 and returns reasoning traces for the training samples.

GLM-5.2 generates 112k output tokens per problem, compared with 33k for Claude-Opus-5, and 82% of the GLM-5.2 tokens are from the 7 replaced calls. Generation of the executable postcondition alone takes 37k output tokens per problem, compared with 7k for Claude-Opus-5.

Results for Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.2 are confounded by prompt revision. Kimi-K3 was run on a revised specification prompt, and one of the 30 problems was rerun on the current prompts, whereas Claude-Opus-5, Claude-Sonnet-5, and both DeepSeek models were run on the earlier revision. For GLM-5.2, 10 problems were run on the earlier revision and 20 on revised versions of 4 of the 5 planning and generation prompts, and the GLM-5.2 repair and token counts therefore mix a model difference with a prompt difference.

G.8.2 Planner

The implementation plan selects the algorithm after both postconditions are accepted, and implementation generation follows the plan. Since errors in the implementation plan are frozen into the file, we measure the plans themselves.

Each of 30 problems was planned once by each candidate, from planning inputs recorded during synthesis. We selected the problems whose implementations had previously relied on a fuel-bounded recursion. Since 26 of the 30 problems are hard, the error counts below describe hard problems. Planning and judging run without compilation, whereas an end-to-end comparison takes a pool of compilation servers and about an hour per candidate.

Kimi-K3 plans fail most often at parsing, before judge review (Table 34). 20 of 30 Kimi-K3 replies were valid JSON, compared with 29 and 30 for both DeepSeek-V4 variants, and all unparsable replies stop before the length limit. A plan that does not parse costs a retry and then the problem.

Each failure mode corresponds to one numbered planning rule, and plans are judged by the same rules that guided planning. A failure mode is recorded for a plan only when the judge names a concrete witness (e.g., an input on which a bound fails, an input size a stated cost cannot handle, a definition generated a second time). We count the failure modes over the plans that parsed (Table 35).

  • •

    Counter. A termination argument based on a counter that the algorithm introduces.

  • •

    Mismatch. A stated running time that belongs to a different algorithm from the planned algorithm.

  • •

    Infeasible. A stated running time beyond the input bounds, under which the test cases cannot finish in compiled evaluation.

  • •

    Ungrounded. A regenerated specification definition with a reason other than cost or a different decided property.

  • •

    Shallow. A specification definition replaced as deciding the wrong property, with no finer definition named for reuse.

  • •

    Search. An algorithm that evaluates the executable postcondition on candidate outputs and returns an accepted candidate.

The plans were judged again by DeepSeek-V4-Pro to measure how far the counts depend on the judge. Both judges are also planning candidates and may favor plans generated by the same model. Under the second judge, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash swap places and Kimi-K3 ranks below both. Only the parse rate is independent of the judge, and the comparison between DeepSeek-V4-Pro and DeepSeek-V4-Flash rests on the parse rate.

G.8.3 Judge

DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, run on the same 79 parsed plans, agree on 97% of the per-mode calls and on 82% of the verdicts. Since a plan counts as clean only when all modes are unflagged, a disagreement on any single mode can change the verdict.

Failure-mode counts depend on the choice of judge, with per-mode agreement over the plans marked by either judge between 0% and 75% (Table 36). DeepSeek-V4-Pro reports Mismatch 3 times and DeepSeek-V4-Flash never, and neither judge reports Ungrounded or Search on any of the 79 plans, so no agreement can be computed for those modes.

The judge model is DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the model of the production quality gates. The second judge bounds the dependence of the reported counts on that inheritance, which a single-judge table cannot show. The agreement reported here is on planner verdicts.

Appendix H Proofs

H.1 Method

We prove the postcondition equivalence theorems with a decompose-and-prove loop, which is a widely adopted strategy for formal proofs (Jiang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b), run by a main agent and a set of subagents (Figure 23).

The main agent holds the queue of problems and hands a problem to one subagent, together with the form of the executable postcondition and the proofs of the closest problems already proved.

The subagent compares the postcondition and the executable postcondition and produces a proof sketch (Jiang et al., 2023), which records the structure common to both postconditions and states one lemma for each remaining clause. The lemmas are given sorry bodies and the file is compiled once, which checks that the lemmas close the theorem before any lemma is proved (Li et al., 2026b). A decomposition that fails is restated by the same subagent, since the next decomposition is built from the open goal. The subagent then proves the lemmas one at a time against the compiler, and each proof is verified against the frozen statement with SafeVerify (GasStationManager, 2024), bumped to Lean 4.32, which checks that no declaration of the problem was changed and that the theorem depends on the standard axioms only.

H.2 Postcondition equivalence theorem

We analyze the proofs by the form of the executable postcondition (Appendix G.2), since the form fixes the statement of the theorem. Executable postconditions that evaluate the postcondition through a decidability instance agree with the postcondition by construction. Separate definitions replace a quantifier of the postcondition by a computation, and the postcondition equivalence proof shows that the replacement loses nothing on valid inputs. The computation is an enumeration that stands in for a set, a reformulation that decides a different property, or a bound that stands in for an unbounded quantifier. The decidable form covers 56% of easy problems and 21% of hard problems, and the proof effort concentrates on the harder problems (Table 37).

A hard proof costs more lemmas rather than more repair rounds (Table 38). Of the 677 problems with a per-problem record, the first compilation of the decomposition passed for 78%, and the median proof took 2 compilations. The median number of lemmas grows from 5 on easy problems to 21 on hard problems while the number of compilations stays at 1 to 2, which places the cost of a hard problem in stating the lemmas and not in repairing the lemmas. The number of lemmas tracks proof length (Spearman 0.96) and compilations are independent of proof length (0.09). A subagent spends a median of 128k tokens, 26 tool calls and 473 seconds on one problem (351 problems with a usage record), and tokens follow proof length (0.71). All 3,037 proofs depend on propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice only. A full replay verified 3,033 proofs and returned no verdict for 4, which match the original except for compiler-generated auxiliary declarations.

The postcondition form and the topic of a problem predict proof length better than difficulty does (Figures 24 and 25). LeetCode difficulty predicts proof length weakly (Spearman 0.31 over all problems), and the topic tags that LeetCode assigns to a problem predict proof length better (Xia et al., 2025). Among separate definitions of medium difficulty, graph problems have a median proof length of 324 lines and two-pointer problems 66. Graph problems state reachability as the existence of a path in the postcondition and compute a closure in the executable postcondition, and the proof relates path and closure by induction on the search. Window problems quantify over the same contiguous ranges in both postconditions, and the proof is index arithmetic. Minimization costs more than maximization, with a median of 179 lines for IsLeast postconditions, compared with 93 for IsGreatest. The candidate set of a maximum is bounded by the input, whereas the lower bound of a minimum is bounded by the precondition alone, and the precondition is invoked in 58% of IsLeast proofs, compared with 39% of IsGreatest proofs. 121 proofs exceed 500 lines and 9 exceed 1,000, all on graph, geometry or string-rewriting problems.

A proof attempt that fails for a reason other than proof difficulty exposes a statement error through a counterexample or through independence. A counterexample is a valid input on which the postcondition and the executable postcondition disagree, and the negation of the theorem is then proved. Independence arises when the executable postcondition evaluates a Float operation, which Lean treats as opaque. Statement errors were found in 31 problems (1.0%), 5 by independence and 26 by a compiled counterexample (Table 39). Each was repaired by the smallest change to the statement that agrees with the problem description, the repaired file passed the frozen test cases, and the theorem was then proved. With the postcondition equivalence theorems proved, the postcondition and executable postcondition of each problem agree on valid inputs. The proofs relate the 2 postconditions to each other, and the human review checks both against the problem description (Appendix I.1).

H.3 Correctness theorem

The correctness theorem asserts that the implementation satisfies the postcondition. Most proofs establish the postcondition directly, and 8 of the 300 proofs show that the implementation satisfies the executable postcondition and transfer the result through the postcondition equivalence theorem. The loop of Appendix H.1 is unchanged.

Correctness theorems are proved for all 300 test problems (72 easy, 155 medium, 73 hard) on the files repaired after the review of Appendix I.1, where 274 proofs are checked under Lean 4.32 and 26 come from the earlier proving run. Correctness proofs grow with difficulty, from a median of 63 lines on easy problems to 178 on medium problems and 365 on hard problems, with a median of 159.5 lines over all 300 problems. All 300 reference implementations are also tested against the executable postcondition with Plausible (Lean Community, 2024), which finds no counterexample (214 pass and 86 are inconclusive, since valid inputs are rarely sampled for structured types).

H.4 Equivalence of accepted outputs

Acceptance relies on test cases and judges, so we also validate accepted SpecGen outputs by proof. For each model in Table 4 and each problem with an accepted output, we draw an accepted output at random and prove its postcondition equivalence theorem. The fixed tactics of the corpus proofs, such as simp with the executable postcondition unfolded, close 557 of the 2,012 drawn outputs in one line (27.7%). The proving loop (Appendix H.1) then settles every remaining output of the 2 RL models and up to 40 remaining outputs of each other model (Table 40). Each attempt ends in a proof or in a counterexample on a valid input, except when a Float operation makes the theorem independent, so no output stays undecided for lack of proof effort.

The theorem is proved for 99.2% of accepted outputs of both RL models (251/253 for AuXSpec-27B-RL and 246/248 for AuXSpec-9B-RL), and all proofs pass SafeVerify under the criteria of the corpus proofs (Appendix H.1). The 6 counterexamples locate the error on both sides of the theorem, in 3 declarative postconditions, 2 executable postconditions and 1 validity predicate, which admits unbalanced inputs for Remove Outermost Parentheses (AuXSpec-9B-RL).

Appendix I Human study

We conduct two human evaluations: a review of the 300 AuXSpec-Test reference problems (Appendix I.1) and an expert review of automatically accepted SpecGen model outputs (Appendix I.2).

I.1 Human review of AuXSpec-Test

The human review of the 300 AuXSpec-Test problems is compared with the errors found while proving (Appendix H.2).

One of the authors, with experience in Lean, reviewed all 300 AuXSpec-Test problems. Each component was compared with the problem description in the order of Table 41. The reviewer was given the Lean file and the description and consulted no model or automated judge. An error was recorded only with an exposing test case, an analysis in prose, and a corrected file that compiles and passes the frozen test suite.

Errors were confirmed in 22 of 300 problems (7.3%), 21 by the review and 1 by the proof of the correctness theorem. The counts by component and difficulty are in Table 42. The postcondition and the implementation account for 20 of the 23 component errors, and the review found no executable postcondition that accepts different outputs from the postcondition. The error rate is highest for easy problems at 9.7% and decreases to 5.5% for hard problems, and 2 of the 3 precondition errors fall on easy problems. Of the 73 files the review changed, 21 changed a definition and the others changed prose or test cases.

Review and proving find different errors. Of the 14 specification errors in the test split, attributed by the order of discovery, 9 were found by review alone and had a postcondition equivalence theorem proved against the wrong statement before the review, since an executable postcondition that decides a wrong postcondition still agrees with the wrong postcondition. 3 were found by both, with compiled counterexamples from the proof attempts. 2 were found by proof attempts alone and had passed the review. In one, the clause ∀i,i<n→A↔B\forall i,\ i<n\to A\leftrightarrow B parses as ∀i,(i<n→A)↔B\forall i,\ (i<n\to A)\leftrightarrow B, and the postcondition therefore rejects all outputs while the text reads correctly. In the other, the executable postcondition compares distances in Float, and the theorem is independent of the axioms. The 10 implementation errors do not affect the postcondition equivalence theorem and are the subject of the correctness theorems of Appendix H.3. Review measures agreement with the problem description, and proving measures agreement between the postcondition and executable postcondition (Table 43). Neither measure subsumes the other, and the dataset was checked by both.

I.2 Expert review of SpecGen evaluation

We review false positives of the automatic SpecGen evaluation for the 2 reported RL checkpoints, AuXSpec-27B-RL and AuXSpec-9B-RL. For each model, we draw 50 problems counted as SpecGen successes, stratified as 12 easy, 26 medium and 12 hard in the proportion of AuXSpec-Test, and review 1 accepted output per problem. Both reviewers each review 60 problems, of which 20 overlap, and the review package masks model identity, judge verdicts, test results against the reference and proof results. Before the review, we test each output against the reference with Plausible, as for the reference implementations (Appendix H.3).

  1. 1.

    Completeness. Plausible samples valid inputs and checks that the executable postcondition accepts the output of the reference implementation. A counterexample is a correct output that the specification rejects.

  2. 2.

    Validity. Plausible samples inputs and checks that the validity predicate agrees with the reference validity predicate. A counterexample is an input that one predicate admits and the other rejects.

We apply the specification-side rubric of Table 41.

Expert review confirms 90 of the 100 accepted outputs, 43 of AuXSpec-27B-RL and 47 of AuXSpec-9B-RL (Table 44). The 2 reviewers find 7 and 5 errors in their 60 problems and agree on all 20 shared problems, including the same 2 errors. Each error comes with a concrete input that the validity predicate admits outside the constraints, which makes the verdict checkable rather than a judgment. All declarative and executable postconditions are correct, and all 10 errors were found in the validity predicate. The missing constraints are guarantees that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer (3 problems), value ranges and alphabets (3), structural guarantees on the input (3) and a time format (1). The postconditions of these outputs therefore remain faithful on every input that the constraints admit. The tests against the reference miss these errors, since random inputs rarely reach the boundary of a missing constraint.

We acknowledge that the expert review covers only 100 outputs which is a small sample, yet the errors found converge to the same kind. The models produce correct postconditions but are highly likely to miss boundary conditions of the constraints in the validity predicate. One possible reason is that the acceptance criteria offer little guidance on the validity predicate, since the specification quality judge assigns clauses that restrict the input to the validity predicate without checking them (Appendix K.3) and only the test layers L1 and L1b check the validity predicate on a few inputs (Table 7). Checking the validity predicate against the stated constraints is a direction for future work (Appendix J).

Appendix J Limitations

Despite the contributions of AuXSpec to specification generation in Lean, the work has several limitations that we hope to address in future work.

Repair at inference. The repair tasks train the models on failed rollouts and are evaluated for a single round (Table 4), and the same tasks support a self-refinement loop at inference, where the model repairs an output on compiler messages and test results over several rounds (Ye et al., 2026b). Pass rates over rounds would show how much of the gap to frontier models such a loop closes.

Scope of expert review. A single reviewer covers the 300 AuXSpec-Test problems and finds errors in 21 of them, including 9 specification errors in problems with a proved postcondition equivalence theorem (Appendix I.1), and 2 reviewers review 100 accepted SpecGen outputs of the RL models (Appendix I.2). The training problems are checked by test cases, judges and postcondition equivalence proofs without review and need a reviewed sample to estimate the error rate of the training data.

Proofs for generated outputs. Generated specifications and implementations are accepted without proofs of the two theorems (Section 2). We prove the postcondition equivalence theorem afterwards for the accepted outputs of the RL models (Appendix H.4). A proof shows only that the 2 postconditions agree. Whether the declarative postcondition and the validity predicate state the problem still rests on test cases, judges and expert review.

Validity predicates. All errors found by the expert review of accepted outputs are input constraints missing from the validity predicate (Appendix I.2). The acceptance criteria check the validity predicate only with test cases. A judge that compares the validity predicate with the stated constraints would cover this part in synthesis, training and evaluation.
